meta.title: Who really said "The Price of Fame Is Not Being Able to Go to the Pub for a Quiet Pint"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Pinned on John Lennon, but undocumented. The oldest trace is Philip Norman's 1981 book Shout! — his narration of a 1966 talk, not Lennon's words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Price of Fame Is Not Being Able to Go to the Pub for a Quiet Pint'?
meta.ogDescription: No Lennon interview, letter or recording contains this line. It hardened out of a 1981 biography's narration about a Liverpool pub and a quiet pint.

answer.label: Not John Lennon’s words — a paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1940–1980 · English musician and songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles
answer.sourceLine: No interview, letter, broadcast or recording has ever been found in which Lennon speaks this sentence. The oldest trace anyone has located is Philip Norman’s 1981 biography Shout! The Beatles in Their Generation, where it is Norman’s own narration of a December 1966 conversation with Lennon’s art-school friend Bill Harry — not a quotation — and the tidy “price of fame” sentence only assembled itself in print decades later.

source.heading: Where the words actually come from

The biographer’s narration — no quotation marks, and two pubs named, not one

source.excerpt: Writing about Lennon’s return to Liverpool in December 1966, Philip Norman describes him confiding to his old art-school friend Bill Harry that he would give anything to walk into a pub like the Philharmonic or Ye Cracke and stand under the chandeliers — in Norman’s phrase, “just having a quiet pint”.
source.trailTitle: How a sentence acquired its quotation marks
trail: 1981 — the earliest known trace. Philip Norman’s Shout! The Beatles in Their Generation (Simon & Schuster, New York) puts the wish for “a quiet pint” in a chapter on December 1966, as narration rather than speech, and names the Philharmonic or Ye Cracke. Quote Investigator verified page 260 on paper ↗

1992 — still not a quotation. Jib Fowles’s Starstruck: Celebrity Performers and the American Public (Smithsonian Institution Press, p. 138) retells it as narration: returning to Liverpool for a concert, Lennon confided to an old chum that he would love to go out to a pub and have a quiet pint. Cited and quoted by QI ↗

2000 — it becomes a quote. A Let’s Go: Europe guide’s Liverpool pub section is the first source QI finds that puts words in Lennon’s mouth — and the wording is “not being able to get a quiet pint at the Phil”, not the sentence circulating today. See QI’s citation, p. 183 ↗

2013 — the search for a source comes up empty. The beer writers Boak & Bailey went hunting and reported that they could not find any reference to where or when Lennon was supposed to have said it, only websites quoting websites; their query is what sent the case to Quote Investigator. Read their post ↗
source.excerptNote: That fragment is the whole of the documentary basis for the modern quotation. Norman does not attribute a sentence to Lennon, offers two pubs rather than one, and says nothing about the price of fame; in his revised 2005 edition he keeps the quiet pint but relocates it to Ye Cracke alone.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator’s full chronology of the ‘quiet pint’ line

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can honestly be asserted for the sentence itself: it is not documented in any Lennon interview, letter, lyric or recording, so there is no identified author or first publication to attach rights to. The nearest documented text is not Lennon’s at all but Philip Norman’s narration in Shout! The Beatles in Their Generation (Simon & Schuster, 1981), which is firmly in copyright to its author and publishers — which is why only a short fragment of it is reproduced above.

author.name: John Lennon
author.kicker: The man it is pinned on
author.heading: John Lennon — and the friend the story really came through
author.metaLine: 1940–1980 · English musician, songwriter and peace activist; co-founder of the Beatles
author.bio: John Winston Ono Lennon (9 October 1940 – 8 December 1980) was an English musician and songwriter who co-founded the Beatles and went on to a substantial solo career. He came up through the Liverpool College of Art, where his fellow students included Bill Harry, who founded the Merseyside music paper Mersey Beat, and Stuart Sutcliffe — the three of them regulars at Ye Cracke on Rice Street, where Lennon also courted Cynthia Powell. That biography matters here: the “quiet pint” story is a Liverpool art-school story, and it reached print through Harry rather than through anything Lennon published or recorded.

misattribution.heading: What the popular version gets wrong
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong person. It is a case of a biographer’s sentence being promoted, step by step, into a quotation — and picking up a sharper shape at every step.

items.why: The earliest source for the “quiet pint” wish is Philip Norman’s Shout! (1981), and Norman presents it as his own narration of what Lennon confided to Bill Harry — not as Lennon’s speech. Quote Investigator, which verified page 260 on paper, notes exactly this ↗.

That formula does not appear in the 1981, 1992 or 2000 retellings. The earliest instance Quote Investigator documents is a 30 August 2008 Observer piece on historic pubs — and even there it is reported speech, and the wording ends “for a drink”, not “for a quiet pint”. QI reproduces the passage ↗.

Norman’s 1981 text names two pubs, the Philharmonic or Ye Cracke. His revised 2005 edition drops the Philharmonic and puts the pint in Ye Cracke instead. The single-pub, “the Phil” version that circulates today is the travel-guide and newspaper form. Both editions are quoted side by side by QI ↗.

items.who: Researchers’ shorthand, not a recorded phrase
items.why: Neither form is documented as Lennon’s speech, but note that the version ending “go to the pub for a quiet pint” is the title Quote Investigator gave its own article ↗ — a researcher’s heading. The wording actually in circulation says “the Phil”.

A line this famous would normally at least appear under “Disputed” or “Misattributed”. Wikiquote’s Lennon page ↗ carries no mention of a pint, a pub, the Philharmonic, Ye Cracke or the price of fame in any section.

misattribution.truthLine: The feeling is plausibly Lennon’s and reached print through his art-school friend Bill Harry; the sentence is not. Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that there is “some evidence” Lennon made such a remark circa 1966, while the phrasing and the identity of the pub “were uncertain” ↗ — and that the earliest citation known to it, 1981, is “rather late”.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: Liverpool tells this story about itself, and it is a good story. The Philharmonic Dining Rooms on Hope Street — “the Phil” — is a Victorian gin-palace of mosaic floors, wrought iron and carved panelling, five minutes from the art college where Lennon was a student. The line hands you the whole arc of a life in one sentence: the boy who could drink there, the Beatle who could not.

The trouble is that the sentence is doing work no source supports. What Philip Norman actually wrote in 1981 was looser and sadder — Lennon, back in Liverpool in December 1966 and confined to dressing rooms, telling Bill Harry he would give anything to stand in a pub like the Philharmonic or Ye Cracke “just having a quiet pint”. There are no quotation marks around it, and there are two pubs, not one. Everything epigrammatic about the modern version was added by other people, later.
context.detailsSummary: How a biographer’s sentence turned into a quotation
detailsBody: The chain is unusually easy to see. In 1981 Norman narrates the wish. In 1992 the media scholar Jib Fowles retells it in Starstruck, still as narration: Lennon “confided to an old chum” that he would love a quiet pint. In 2000 a Let’s Go: Europe travel guide is, on Quote Investigator’s evidence, the first to put the words inside quotation marks — and gives them as “not being able to get a quiet pint at the Phil”. In 2008 an Observer pub piece supplies the “price of fame” framing, but as reported speech, and says “for a drink”. The sentence that now circulates has the 2008 framing welded to the 1981 pint — a combination that appears in none of them.

Norman himself did not hold the detail steady. When he revised Shout! in 2005 he dropped the Philharmonic altogether and set the longed-for pint in Ye Cracke, under the mural of Wellington meeting Blücher. A quote whose own earliest source changes the pub between editions is not a quote anyone should be putting in quotation marks.

The beer writers Jessica Boak and Ray Bailey went looking for a primary source in 2013 and came up empty, wondering aloud whether the real author was “a clever brewery PR man or pub landlord”. Their query is what prompted Quote Investigator to take the case; QI’s guess is that the testimony began with Bill Harry, who wrote prolifically about the Beatles, but no Harry article or interview carrying the line has yet been found.
context.pull: Norman never put it in quotation marks. Everyone since has.

schema.verdictNote: Attributed to John Lennon, but no interview, letter, broadcast or recording documents him saying it. The earliest trace is Philip Norman's 1981 book Shout!, where the wish for a quiet pint is the biographer's own narration rather than a quotation. There is some evidence Lennon made a remark of this kind around 1966, but the wording in circulation is not his and should be treated as unattributed.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator examined "The price of fame is not being able to go to the Phil for a quiet pint", found the earliest relevant evidence in Philip Norman's 1981 Shout! (chapter 14, December 1966, p. 260, Simon & Schuster, verified on paper), noted Norman did not present a direct quote and named two pubs, cited Fowles's Starstruck 1992 p. 138, Let's Go: Europe 2000 p. 183 as the first direct-quotation form ("not being able to get a quiet pint at the Phil"), the 2005 revised Shout! p. 294 relocating the pint to Ye Cracke, and a 30 August 2008 Observer piece with the "price of fame ... to the Phil for a drink" reported-speech wording; and concluded there is "some evidence" of such a remark circa 1966 while "the phrasing of the comment and the identity of the pub were uncertain" and the 1981 citation is "rather late". QI conjectures Bill Harry was the source. QI's own article title uses "the Pub".

Boak & Bailey's 4 April 2013 post reports that "we can't find any reference to where or when Lennon is supposed to have said the above", that "some websites quote other websites", that the earliest print reference they could find via Google Books was the Let's Go guide to Europe from 2000, and wonders whether the attribution ought to belong to "a clever brewery PR man or pub landlord".

Boak & Bailey's 5 August 2014 follow-up quotes Quote Investigator's conclusion ("there is some evidence that circa 1966 John Lennon made a remark about the difficulty of experiencing a 'quiet pint' in a favorite Liverpool pub"), states QI traced it back as far as Philip Norman's 1981 biography Shout! "but not to source", and appeals for copies of magazines containing Bill Harry's early Beatles writing.

Wikiquote's John Lennon page contains no occurrence of "pint", "pub", "Philharmonic", "Phil", "Ye Cracke" or "price of fame" in any section, including its Disputed and Misattributed sections. (Verified twice: by fetching the rendered page and by grepping the raw wikitext via action=raw — zero matches.)
John Winston Ono Lennon (born John Winston Lennon; 9 October 1940 – 8 December 1980) was an English musician, songwriter and activist, a founding member of the Beatles.

Bill Harry (born 17 September 1938) founded Mersey Beat and attended the Liverpool College of Art, where his fellow students included John Lennon and Stuart Sutcliffe; the three often spent time together at the Cracke pub in Rice Street.

Ye Cracke is a 19th-century pub on Rice Street, Liverpool; John Lennon and Stuart Sutcliffe were regulars there when they studied at the nearby art college, and it was there that Lennon courted his first wife, Cynthia Powell.

The Internet Archive holds a copy of Philip Norman's Shout!: The Beatles in Their Generation, published New York: Simon & Schuster, 1981 (confirmed via archive.org's metadata API: creator "Norman, Philip, 1943-", publisher "New York : Simon & Schuster", date 1981; the details page returns HTTP 200).

The Philharmonic Dining Rooms in Liverpool were built 1898–1900 and are a listed building. NOTE: this page does NOT mention John Lennon or any quote about fame or a quiet pint — it is therefore NOT used anywhere on this page as support for the quotation, and is not included in externalLinks.
